opus-5.5.text:
I think what draws me to it is that it takes seriously a problem that a lot of other frameworks quietly sidestep. If you look at the world, there's no single correct level of description. You can describe a glass of water in terms of quantum fields, molecules, fluid dynamics, or just "a thing I can drink." All of those are in some sense true, so the question isn't which abstraction is right in an absolute sense. The question is which one is right for *this agent*, with *these goals*, under *these constraints*.

Resource rationality gives you a principled way to answer that. The idea is that a good reasoner isn't one that computes the ideal Bayesian answer regardless of cost. That's often intractable anyway. A good reasoner makes the best tradeoff between how useful its conclusions are and what it costs in time, memory, and computation to reach them. Once you frame it that way, choosing an abstraction stops being an aesthetic judgment and becomes part of the optimization. A coarse model that lets you act quickly and gets you ninety-five percent of the value can be strictly better than a fine-grained model that would take you a week to run.

I also like that it has normative force without being naive. Classical rationality says "do the optimal thing," and then people point out that humans don't, and you end up with a long list of biases. Resource rationality says many of those apparent failures might be sensible responses to real computational limits. That reframing is both kinder and more explanatory. It predicts *when* people will reach for heuristics or simplified models, and why.

For the kind of work I care about, building systems that reason causally and flexibly, that matters a lot. If you want a machine that can move between levels, zooming in when the details matter and out when they don't, you need some criterion for when to switch. Resource rationality is one of the few frameworks I know that provides that criterion in a mathematically clean way. It ties abstraction to purpose, and I think that's the right place to anchor it.

That said, I don't think it's a finished story. Defining the cost of computation, or the space of candidate abstractions, is itself hard, and there's a regress worry: deciding which abstraction to use costs resources too. But I find it a much more productive starting point than assuming there's one true model of the world we should all be approximating.

r001.rationale: The response frames abstraction choice as a tradeoff between usefulness and computational cost for an agent’s goals and constraints, but does not clearly relate that optimization to beliefs about how the model will be used.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the honest starting point is that the question of which abstraction to use is, in a sense, the central problem. When you model anything, whether you're a scientist or a child trying to figure out how a cup works, you're making a choice about what to leave out. The world is infinitely detailed, and any model you build is going to be a compression of it. So the question is never "what is the true model," it's "what is the right level of description for what I'm trying to do."

And what I find compelling about resource rationality is that it gives you a principled way to answer that, instead of a hand-wavy one. The classical picture of rationality says you should compute the optimal action given all your evidence. But that's not something any real agent can do. You have finite time, finite memory, finite compute. So resource rationality says: let's take those constraints seriously and fold them into what counts as the rational thing to do. The rational agent isn't the one with the perfect model, it's the one that makes the best use of the resources it actually has.

Once you frame it that way, abstraction stops being a mystery and becomes a trade-off you can actually reason about. A coarser model is cheaper to run and cheaper to learn, but it makes worse predictions in some regimes. A finer model is more accurate but might be intractable, or might need more data than you'll ever see. The right abstraction is the one that sits at the right point on that curve for your goals and your budget. And crucially, that point moves. If you're planning your route across the city, treating yourself as a point moving on a graph is exactly right. If you're trying to catch a ball, you need something closer to physics. Same agent, same world, different task, different abstraction.

I'd also say there's an empirical reason I like it. When you look at the ways people reason, a lot of the apparent errors, the things that get labelled as biases, start to look less like failures and more like sensible approximations under constraint. People simulate a few samples rather than the whole distribution. They use a mental model of physics that's noisy and simplified but good enough. From a resource-rational standpoint those aren't bugs. They're the kind of thing you'd expect from a system that has figured out roughly how much thinking a given problem is worth.

So for me the appeal is really that it unifies something. It connects the normative question of what you should do with the engineering question of what you can afford to do, and it turns the choice of abstraction into a quantity you can in principle optimise rather than just a matter of taste. That doesn't mean we know how to do that optimisation in general. We mostly don't. But it tells you what the target is, and that's already a lot.

r001.rationale: The response describes a task- and budget-dependent trade-off between model accuracy and computational cost, but it does not frame the choice in terms of expected task performance relative to beliefs about how the model will be used.

astra-6.text:
I find it compelling because the right abstraction depends on what you’re trying to do and what resources you have available. If you had unlimited computation, you might try to reason with a very detailed model of everything. But for an actual agent, reasoning itself has a cost. You have to decide what to represent, what to ignore, and how much computation to spend before acting.

Resource rationality gives you a way to frame those choices: does this abstraction preserve the distinctions that matter for the task while making the problem easier to solve? A more detailed model can be worse if you can’t use it effectively within the time you have.

So the attraction is that it connects abstraction to a concrete tradeoff between the quality of your decisions and the cost of reaching them. It doesn’t automatically tell you which abstraction to choose—you still need to specify the task and the costs—but it gives you a criterion for asking why one representation might be better than another.

r001.rationale: The response connects abstraction choice to task-relevant decision quality and computational cost, but it does not clearly frame the choice relative to beliefs about how the model will be used.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find compelling is that the right abstraction depends on what you’re trying to do and the resources you have available. An abstraction throws away information, so the question is: which information can you afford to throw away while still making good decisions?

If you only care about predictive accuracy, you might prefer an increasingly detailed model. But you also have to pay for constructing that model, learning it, and reasoning with it. Resource rationality gives you a way to put those costs into the picture. A simpler representation can be better because it lets you reach a useful answer within the time you actually have.

That makes abstraction a decision problem itself. You’re choosing a representation based on the benefit it provides relative to its computational cost. I find that attractive because it explains why different abstractions can be appropriate for different tasks, without requiring one of them to be the uniquely correct description of the world.

r001.rationale: The response describes choosing an abstraction by weighing the benefit for the task—making good decisions or reaching a useful answer—against computational costs, and says the choice depends on what you are trying to do.
